The Honourable, the Speaker of the House of Commons, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Speaker:
I enclose herewith my resignation as member of the house. This course, severing as it does many happy associations, I find necessary owing to my acceptance of the chairmanship of the Liquor Control Board of Ontario.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect
to the communication which you have just read I should like to assure my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Bennett) that all of us on this side of the house join very sincerely with him in regretting the resignation of Sir Henry Drayton as a member of the house. While Sir Henry Drayton was opposed to us politically, and differed from us on many matters of political opinion, differences were usually so expressed as not to tend to lessen the ties of friendship existing between hon. members on both sides of the house. I might almost say that no member of the house had more personal friends among members of all political parties than the member for West York. Sir Henry some years ago in order to serve his country in parliament resigned the position of chairman of the railway commission, a very
fMr. Mackenzie King.]

Resignation of Sir Henry Drayton
important position in the public service of Canada. He did so, I believe, from the highest and most public spirited of motives, and since that time he has continuously served in parliament as a minister of the crown or an honourable member of this house. Sir Henry is now returning to duties somewhat similar in character to those he discharged on the railway commission. As chairman of another very important commission, I am sure he will bring to his new task that exceptional personal and professional equipment which marked his tenure of office as chairman of the railway commission. We all wish him every success in his new field of public service.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
On behalf of myself and those
associated with me who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, I desire to thank the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) very sincerely for the kind references he has made to Sir Henry Drayton, who until a few moments ago was the member for West York. With all that the Prime Minister has said with respect to Sir Henry Drayton, it is of course our delight to agree. To his public duties he brought a highly trained mind. He was an experienced lawyer and an able administrator, and his experience as chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners gave him an insight into Canadian business, and a knowledge of conditions throughout the country, unrivalled at the time he accepted the very onerous and responsible duties of Minister of Finance of Canada. At that time it was exceedingly difficult to induce any man of standing to undertake so large a responsibility, having regard to the then condition of our country. Sir Henry Drayton had, as the Prime Minister has said, a very high sense of his duty to Canada, and the discharge of that duty occasioned him .a great deal of worry and anxiety. Like most public men, now that his*services in this chamber have ceased they are more truly recognized at their real worth, alike by his friends and his opponents. I am sure we are very deeply grateful to the Prime Minister and those who sit with him for the kindly references they have made to our colleague, and their appreciation of what the house has lost. His departure, however regrettable it may be to members of the house generally, will be much more keenly felt by those of us who have been so intimately associated with him in parliament.

We in this comer of the house desire to be associated with other members in expressing our regret at the resignation of the hon. member for West York, Sir Henry Drayton. It is quite true that Sir Henry has given very valuable service to his country, and while he is leaving this particular field, in which he had laboured so long and faithfully, he is nevertheless available for public service in another direction. When I first came to this house some years ago I think I received more encouragement from Sir Henry Drayton than from practically any other member of the house, and I shall always remember with great appreciation his kindly manner on all occasions. Once again I wish to say on behalf of those who sit with me how heartily we associate ourselves with other members in the house in this expression of appreciation of Sir Henry Drayton.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING CONTINUANCE OP AID TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
At the time of the con-
Technical Education

ference between the members of the federal government and the provincial premiers and ministers the whole question of grants in aid of provincial undertakings was very fully discussed, It was the general view of the premiers and ministers of the provinces that they would like to receive in the form of a direct subsidy anything to which they were entitled in the way of aid from the federal treasury. They took the view that a grant from the federal government carrying with it an obligation on the part of the provincial governments to undertake part of the work was frequently embarrassing, and that on the whole it was not good policy that grants should be made conditional by the federal government. I must say that the representations of the provinces in that particular were pretty generally assented to; it was I believe the general consensus of view that the provinces should deal wholly with these matters, which come primarily within their jurisdiction, and that if the federal treasury were to assist them in any way the assistance should be by way of subsidy grant, thus allowing the provinces to dispose of the funds as they deem best.
With regard to the Technical Education Act, as my hon. friend knows, the intention as expressed at the time the act was introduced was to make from the federal treasury a contribution only over a period of years, primarily with the object of helping the provinces to inaugurate a system of technical education, and secondarily to insure in whatever they might undertake some degree of sjimmetry and uniformity among the provinces themselves. But it was never contemplated that the federal treasury should continue indefinitely to contribute to technical education. At the recent conference there was considerable discussion on the question of scientific and industrial research which, as my hon. friend knows, is closely allied to that of technical education, and in this connection it was felt that the establishment of scientific research laboratories should be undertaken by the federal government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) has already intimated to this house that the government has decided to ask parliament to make a substantial grant towards establishing in the capital laboratories for scientific and industrial research, to serve the needs of the entire Dominion. We feel that if we undertake this obligation and establish scientific and industrial research laboratories on the scale which is intended-and the decision was reached after discussion with the provinces themselves-we are going as far as we should be expected to go in dealing 
in a combined way with scientific research and technical education.
The aid given under the Technical Education Act does not expire until 1929. It was two or three years ago that the first notification was sent to the provinces that on the expiry of the present act its provisions would not be renewed, and the provinces have had ample opportunity, and still have ample opportunity, to make provision themselves for satisfactorily carrying on the work which has been undertaken. We may consider continuing assistance, for a period of time to correspond with that which the act was originally intended to serve, to provinces that have not taken full advantage of the act, but those that have been receiving aid for the full period of time under the provisions of this act will at the expiration of the act be expected to carry on the work for which this assistance was given them in order to enable them to make a beginning in a satisfactory way.

I think it

It is only part of the broader policy of seeking to have the provinces continue to deal with matters coming primarily within their own jurisdiction, a practice which came to be subject to some considerable variation only during the war period. We feel it is going to be better for all concerned to have the Dominion parliament take care of those matters which are assigned to it under the British North America Act and have the provinces do the same with respect to theirs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is to give the exchequer court jurisdiction in passing-off actions as well as statutory actions for infringements of the Trade Marks and Designs Act. Those actions are common law actions while an infringement action is under a statute. The exchequer court has ruled that under the act as it stands, it has no jurisdiction in common law and has to apply the statute strictly and rigidly. Of course in relations between the crown and the subject when the crown is plaintiff or petitioner, it is specifically stated that the court has jurisdiction at common law or in equity, but in relations between subject and subject the cdurt has no such jurisdiction. On section 4-Practice and procedure, how regulated.

This is not quite consistent with the attitude generally taken by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, to make the practice of the high court of England as it existed on January 1, 1928, applicable to our courts. Would it not be better to let our courts frame their own regulations and have them approved by the governor in Council? It says:

The practice and procedure in suits, actions and matters in the exchequer court, shall, so far as they are applicable, and unless it is otherwise provided for by this act, or by eneral rules made in pursuance of this act, e regulated by the practice and procedure in similar suits, actions and matters in His Majesty's High Court of Justice in England on the first day of January, 1928.
I must say I rather dislike that form of statute. That is only my personal view. We had the same thing in the Northwest Territories, as the minister will recall. I think it would be much better to permit the court to formulate its own rules, regulations and practice, but it might be well, having regard to the desirability of maintaining some uniformity in patent practice throughout the Empire, to say that in no case shall larger powers be conferred upon the judge or court than would be conferred upon them by the rules and regulations in force in England on the 1st day of January, 1928, rather than to have it as it now is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As my hon. friend says, it is merely a question of date. The section already exists in our statute, and we are simply making it January 1, 1928, instead of 1907, because since that date there have been changes in the practice and procedure in England. My hon. friend suggests that it might be better if we had our own rules and regulations, but I would point out that this amendment is suggested by the judges of the exchequer court themselves, in order to make their practice more modern. Probably they will see to it that they have their own rules and regulations.

I am afraid they are not
imbued with nationalist sentiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is wrong.
We are making this change because we want to do it. That is autonomy. We are not being forced to do it; we are doing it of our own free will.
The real effect is merely to say that the exchequer court practice shall be governed by the English practice as of the 1st day of January, 1928?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Exactly, instead of 1907.

The practice of 1907 is,
of course, somewhat antiquated having regard to modern rules that have been made to meet the changed conditions of business, but it does occur to me that it would be easier and simpler to amend our own rules. There is no court in England that is exactly the counterpart of our exchequer court. The high court of justice is divided into the chancery division,

the court of King's Bench, probate, admiralty and divorce, and the chancery division takes these patent oases, and the rules and regulations of the chancery division apply, except in cases otherwise expressly provided for, to all divisions, and would govern this practice. It all comes down to the courts determining whether or not a particular rule in England to meet conditions in England is applicable to conditions in Canada, which personally as a practitioner, now no longer actively engaged,
I used to dislike very much, I think it much better to have our own rules sanctioned by our own court. We had the rules of the English court in the Northwest Territories in the early days, and we found it very inconvenient after a time, and passed our own rules and regulations.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-General rules and orders.

I would suggest to the minister that in paragraph (a) the words "practice and" be inserted before the word "procedure."
I think practice differs in some respect from procedure, and I think the whole matter of practice and procedure should be subject to the general rules, made by the judges in the court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend suggests
using the words used in the previous section. Personally I do not see any strong objection, except that we are here simply using the language which is already in the statute, the only amendment being to say "judges" instead of "judge". We are not changing any other part of the section.

Inasmuch as we are withdrawing the exchequer court so far as possible from the practice and procedure which prevails in His Majesty's high court of justice in England, I think it would be wise to use the words "practice and procedure".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection, and
I move accordingly, Mr. Chairman.

I think the words
"practice and procedure" are the words in general use. The word practice was used by some of the English judges because a practice had grown up that was not governed by their rules and practice, and so they say "practice and procedure" universally in the English rules.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 72, to amend the Fertilizer Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Sections 1 and 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Information to be set forth on brand, etc.

Mr. Chairman, as I explained to the committee on a previous occasion with respect of some other bills introduced by the Minister of Agriculture, I have grave doubts as to their constitutionality. For instance, this bill prohibits sale and possession, and unless it can be said that these powers are ancillary to the general powers over agriculture given to this parliament by the British North America Act, I think the bill would share the fate of the government grading act, in some sections at any rate. I suppose, as the minister said on a former occasion, it might be all right to pass it;-
Take a shot at it.

That it might be all
right to take a shot at it; but I suggest to him that the "shot" might come from another quarter.

Mr. Chairman, I do think
the house should hesitate to pass bills of this character where there is grave doubt as to their being within the legislative competence of this parliament. We are really passing a criminal statute, and it places upon those who are conducting a perfectly legitimate business the burden of carrying to the highest courts of the land the issue of constitutionality, a burden that is almost intolerable. I regret very much that I was not in the house last week when another bill of this description was passed, for I believe it went far beyond our jurisdiction. If I were advising a client I should regard it as perfectly moral as well as legal to counsel him to defy such a statute from the very start. I see no reason why parliament itself should undertake an illegal act; it brings the whole of our statutory law into disrepute and forms an incentive to disregard law generally.

Mr. Chairman, I think the
same point occurred to some members of the committee; but as I understand this bill, it is simply amending an act, and if this measure is beyond the powers of parliament, I think

Fertilizer Act

the act itself is in precisely the same position, and I do not see that we can make things worse by passing the bill.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that on two other occasions I pointed out that several of these bills dealing with
various branches of the Department of Agriculture have this question of constitutionality bound up with them. The original law has been on the statute books a good many years, and we have amended it once or twice, but its constitutionality has never been challenged. Consequently we proceed on the assumption that it is constitutional. The Live Stock Act was challenged on this ground. I immediately got in touch with all the provincial departments of agriculture and with one or two exceptions they passed concurring legislation. Should we meet a similar difficulty with regard to the fertilizer or any other act, then we shall take the same course, and if the provinces want the legislation they will pass the necessary concurring bills. I do not think it is advisable to cross the bridge until we come to it. We have not yet come to the bridge with respect to any of these pieces of legislation with the exception of the Live Stock Act.

The "bridge" to which the
hon. minister refers is well nigh an intolerable bui'de|n for the ordinary 'agriculturist or merchant dealing in fertilizers. Why should you place the burden upon an individual of carrying litigation to the supreme court at a cost of thousands of dollars in order to ascertain whether the law is ultra vires of parliament or not? It seems to me that in respect of agriculture there is a good deal of joint and several jurisdiction, and that it would be wise in all these matters to bring the proposed legislation before the provincial governments and have them, if possible, pass concurrent legislation to dispose of all doubt. But I suggest that the minister, in introducing legislation of this kind, is not assuming a conciliatory attitude in respect of the provincial departments of agriculture, whose co-operation is necessary in order to give validity to his enactment.

That position is well taken, only I happen to have done what is suggested; and I am under promise to do it with respect to the Live Stock Act. The committee on agriculture reported to-day regarding that act. The matter was taken up with the provincial ministers before we even drafted that legislation, and all other similar acts have gone before the Justice department. We have received the best advice they could 
give and in many instances they have even helped to draft the legislation. Why, therefore, should I anticipate that the Justice department is wrong by going to the provincial departments and asking them to delegate to us powers which we may already have, and which, according to the Department of Justice, we have? It is only when these powers are challenged that we should consult the provinces. Suppose I went to the Minister of Agriculture of either Quebec or Ontario and said, "I should like you to pass concurring legislation with respect to this matter". That minister would immediately ask, "Has it been challenged?" If I said, no, he would then ask why I wanted to anticipate difficulty.
We are challenging it now.

The provinces are
jealous of their powers and do not like to delegate them to us unless they want legislation badly enough, and it is only when legislation of this kind is challenged that it becomes necessary to have the powers delegated to us. I have found them agreeable.

Section agreed to.
Sections 4 to 7 inclusive agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed, on division.

Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee on bill No. 51, to regulate the sale and inspection of root vegetables.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.
This bill was amended in the committee, and I do not find on my files a copy of the printed amendment. Unless that is available we cannot discuss the matter intelligently.

I have not a copy of the amendment myself; I did not expect that we should take it up so soon. There ought to be some understanding in regard to the reprinting of these bills wherever they are substantially changed, and the leaders in the house, as well as the member in charge of the bill, should be supplied with copies.

My recollection is that in committee this bill was materially changed. There were several amendments, one of which was particularly important. We should have a copy of the reprint before proceeding.

Root Vegetables Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There are no lengthy
amendments and I will undertake to read each amended clause fully, as we come to it.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Vegetables sold, etc., must comply with this act and regulations.

What I said in connection with the other bill, with respect to the constitutional right of parliament to enact legislation of this character, I now repeat. I do not think we should content ourselves with merely expressing our views privately, but we should publicly point out that there is a grave doubt regarding the constitutional power of this parliament to pass the bill in its present form. Such a statement is necesary in order that it might not be said that there was no one in parliament who apprehended the difficulties in connection with prosecutions that might be brought under such legislation.

This bill also was
submitted to the Justice department, and while there may be some constitutional doubt, as my hon. friend has said, the legislation has never been challenged.

Section 3 is entirely
new.

Why should we not continue the legislation until it is challenged? We have had the best advice from the department, not only under the present but under preceding governments, indicating that we are on sound lines.

Section 3, I say, is entirely new, and it prohibits the sale of vegetables by any person except under special conditions. This I consider an interference with the exclusive powers of the provincial legislatures.
As a rule there are exemptions under all these bills.

Will the minister explain
this bill? It seems to me to impose upon the ordinary agriculturist such intolerable conditions that it would be almost impossible for anyone to carry on the business of diversified farming as it is engaged in in the older provinces. You are making almost every farmer a criminal at the start if he carries on his business in the ordinary way to which he has been accustomed.

There were on the committee a number of practical farmers who did not seem to be alarmed, especially in 56103-144*
view of the exemptions provided in section 21. I was not in the committee at the time, but the suggestion was made, I am informed, that we might provide further exemptions if we found any hardship existing such as my hon. friend fears. Very often when you make an exemption people take advantage of it, so we have taken power to remove some of the exemptions, and if we find in practice that more are desirable we can increase the number. The reason we have extended our power in this respect is that these vegetables change from year to year, just as the commercial grades of western wheat change. In the west we have what is called the western grain standards board, which is given authority to specify grades from year to year according the peculiarities of the grain in that particular year. We find that this works very satisfactorily, and since vegetables also vary we have given the government power to establish grades on the advice of an advisory board according to the peculiarities of the vegetables for the particular year. More than half the grain in the west is dealt with in that way, and it is found to be quite workable. There are certain exemptions here, with which we can deal when we reach them. I do not think this is an occasion for alarm, although looking at this act superficially it does seem arbitrary. However, it is hedged about with enough provisoes that no one will get hurt, so far as I can see.

Will the minister be
good enough to tell us who requested all these regulations?

We found that
when we had a case in court the Department of Justice would invariably show us where the law was weak. This act has not been before the house for five or six years, and the evasions of the law have accumulated during that time. We have been shown how to stop these evasions, and we are doing so by these new sections.
I can assure the minister that this will not be a way to avoid trouble for his government.

As an example let us
consider section 4. Under this section potatoes, onions, turnips, artichokes, beets, carrots and parsnips must be sold by weight. We all know that in markets all over this country, and especially in the older provinces, during one season of the year these articles are all sold in bunches, and later when the roots have matured they are sold by measurement and not by weight. These vegetables are never sold by weight; they are sold by
Root Vegetables Act

the basket, by the peck or by the bushel, but now that is to be changed. I am afraid we will have our standards of weights changed one of these days, if we are not careful; we may find ourselves using the metric system without knowing it.
If my hon. friend had taken the time to read the act through he would have found the exemptions under section 21.
There are not enough exemptions.

We can open it as wide as a barn door if we consider it necessary. My hon. friend should give the committee on agriculture some credit for knowing what they are doing; we thought this was a pretty good bill. There is a constitutional exception which may be taken to it, but this has been in practice from time immemorial.
These sections are new.
Why should we expect that someone is going to gabble us up in this respect?

Why should you pass such a law which will include every market in the city of Montreal? If market gardeners cany on their business in their usual way, under this law our gaols will be filled with these men.
Or we will make a joke of the law.

That is so. The only exceptions made under section 21 deal with new potatoes, seed potatoes, green onions and pickled onions. We who live in apartments are accustomed to go to the market, either personally or by sending someone from the house, to purchase fresh vegetables beginning early in June. The persons who sell those fresh vegetables to us cannot carry on their ordinary business without being subject to these penalties for the commission of criminal offences. If the minister undertakes to enforce that law in the city of Montreal we will have a small revolution on our hands.
Oh, well-

The minister may say, "Oh well", but why should he introduce a measure of this vexatious character which serves no useful end at all? If he is dealing with the export trade of the country and wishes certain grading with respect to that trade, we are prepared to take such a measure into most favourable consideration, but when you say that a person who has a little country place cannot sell a bushel of beets or turnips to his
[Mr. Chaplin.!
neighbour without weighing them, unless he commits a criminal offence, you are proposing ridiculous and preposterous legislation which this house should not favourably consider. The fact is that under the grading system proposed it will be absolutely impossible for the ordinary city market gardener to carry on business.

I admit that that is quite a natural position to be taken by one who has not studied the question; the whole thing looks ridiculous. I will admit that freely, but this law has been applied to potatoes and onions for at least six years, and I have not heard of any Montreal market gardeners being gaoled because of it. We are now extending the principle to other vegetables; that is all we propose to do.
Has the law been enforced during that time?
Of course. Some of these market gardeners have been fined, but I 'do not remember that any of them have gone to gaol, and I have seen no deputations protesting against the law.
I wish to enter my protest against this legislation also.
To which section is my hon. friend referring?

I am referring to sections 3 and 4, and to section 21; perhaps as I go on I may take in a few more. The minister says there are certain provisoes under section 21 which remove from the bill its ridiculous character; he admits that it is ridiculous up to the last section, but states that section 21 removes the ridiculous features. That is one way to legislate. Let us look at that section for a moment, in conjunction with sections 3 and 4. Section 4 provides that potatoes, onions and other vegetables must be sold by weight, and if this is not done the market gardeners are liable to a fine or imprisonment. If a man wants to sell old potatoes they must be sold by weight, but if he is selling new potatoes he can sell them by the dozen or in any other way he may desire, because there is a proviso which protects potatoes coming on the market between July 1 and September 30. Suppose a man has seed potatoes for sale; if he can show that they are certified seed potatoes he may sell them, I suppose, in bulk or by measure, by the dozen or any way he likes.
By the bunch.

Or by the bunch. Why the exception in this particular

Root Vegetables Act
case as compared with old potatoes? As the hon. member (Mr. Cahan) has pointed out, the market gardeners who come into nearly all our cities and towns are accustomed to selling their produce by the dozen or by the bunch; why should they not be allowed to do that? If a man has a cretain quantity of potatoes in bags why should he not be free to enter into a bargain with a buyer who wishes to take them as they are; why must he have them weighed? It seems to me the minister is assuming in this legislation that the people who go to market to buy potatoes, onions, beets and that sort of thing have not brains enough to protect themselves in making bargains with the farmers. All this restrictive legislation is most inconvenient to the farmer. The minister may say that the gaols are not full of farmers who have violated this act, but I venture to say that the government has made no attempt to enforce this part of it which the minister says has been operative for the last six years, otherwise the gaols would foe full, because the people simply cannot conform to an act of this kind. The minister has not told us yet why this provision is necessary; at least if he has I have not heard it. Why does he propose to compel everybody to sell everything by weight? If it were a matter of export then I could understand the weight regulation, but I cannot understand applying such a provision to a little deal between two persons in a market town. Give them credit for a little common sense; do not hedge their operations about with restrictions which make them liable to fine or imprisonment. Will the minister tell us whence came the demand for this legislation?

We had these questions all thoroughly discussed five years ago, but I have no objection to going all over them again. I judge from my hon. friend's remarks that he disapproves of selling by weight. Why is selling by weight necessary? Because we have no standardized bag in this country that I know of in connection with the sale of potatoes or any other vegetables. In some parts of Canada a bag of potatoes means 100 pounds, in others it is 90, 80, or even less. If I order so many bags of potatoes how am I to know what I am getting unless I know how much the bag contains? We have at least four different sizes of potato bags, and we are trying to get down to our recognized standard of weights.

A man is
coming to market with a load of potatoes. He finds when he comes to make up his load that he is short of what you call standard
bags. He has some old sacks and things of that kind, so he fills them up with his potatoes and takes them into the market. Some of the sacks may contain two bushels, some two and a half bushels. Now, if I come along and want to buy those potatoes, and if I am willing to bulk the lot, using my own judgment as to how many potatoes are there, why should I not be permitted to do so? In any case, if I have any doubt about it I always have the right to demand that they be weighed, and if he is anxious to sell he is going to conform to my wishes and let them be weighed. Why tell him, therefore, that he must sell only by weight? An inspector, nosing around to find some justification for his job, sees me enter into that bargain with this farmer. I am satisfied, the farmer is satisfied, but the inspector reports that the farmer sold these potatoes without having weighed them, and he is liable to fine and imprisonment. That is the kind of legislation the government is asking this house to put through. I repeat that it is not only unnecessary, it is ridiculous; and the ridiculous feature of it is not eliminated by section 21.

Well, there is
nothing in the law to prevent a farmer from taking his potatoes to market in two-bushel bags, three-bushel or four-bushel bags, so long as he marks the number of pounds on the bag. We want to encourage selling by weight, which is the only sure way by which the customer may know what he is getting. I cannot imagine that a buyer would take a whole lot of potatoes, say, for 810; that is a hypothetical case-I do not think it would ever actually occur, because a buyer would want to know how many bushels there were in that lot. However, there is nothing in the act that I know of to prevent him from doing that. If it is a practice which may develop -farmers bringing in a load of potatoes and buyers taking them without knowing the size or weight of the load-well then, we will have to make an exemption to permit farmers to do that if they want to. I cannot imagine, however, that they will want to do it. So far as the bag is concerned, one reads the market reports in the newspapers and sees that potatoes were sold at so much a bag, but the size of the bag is seldom given and nobody knows what the exact quantity is. That is why I think weight is the only safe standard.

Everybody
knows the weight of a bag of potatoes.

No, it runs from
70 pounds to 100-many of them more.
Root Vegetables Act

There is a
bushel and a half in a bag, isn't there?

Section 21, which in the
opinion of the minister saves the whole act, sets out that the provisions of the act shall not apply to what are commonly termed "green onions" or other vegetables with top leaves attached. Now if the ordinary market gardener who comes to the village where I am staying for part of the summer sells me carrots with the green leaves attached he is not committing a criminal offence, but if he sells me carrots which have no green leaves on them he is liable to fine and imprisonment unless he carries about with him a scale and weighs them, which is not the ordinary practice of the market gardener. So it would be with parsnips. I see the market gardener going through the country village with his cart, and I wish to buy a peck of parsnips. He may sell me a peck of parsnips if they have the leaves attached, as is very often the case, but if they have not the leaves attached he is liable to fine and imprisonment if he does not comply with this act. It seems ridiculous to make a provision so detailed apply to the market gardener. I am not looking for a political issue on the island of Montreal, but I venture to say that if the government take the responsibility of enacting these provisions into law I can raise a hue and cry throughout the island of Montreal. It would be one of the best political issues I could possibly raise-going to each market gardener throughout that island and telling him how this ridiculous legislation is made to apply to his special business.

My hon. friend is
apparently not familiar with the method of marketing these vegetables. For instance, there is only one way to sell green onions and that is with their tops on. They are little green onions pulled when the onions are immature, tied in bunches and sold at so much a package. I do not know whether that is the way they are sold in Ottawa or not, but that is the authorized practice. When the spring onions mature and the tops come oS in the maturing, they go into storage and later they are sold on the market by weight.
But the carrot leaves do not come off?
They do not come off when the carrots are pulled up first. When they are young carrots, they are sold in the same way as green onions.

You have not exempted
green carrots.

Anything that is
green is sold with the tops on.
Do pickling onions go to market with the tops on?
What are commonly known as pickling onions, silver-skin onions, are exempted.
Why favour them?

Because there is a
small, special variety for pickling onions.

They can
sell them by the dozen. They will not have any green tops on them.

Does my hon.
friend not want us to exempt them? Because if he does not, we do not need to. If we find later on that the exemption is being abused, we can remove it.

Am I to
understand from that that the minister will accept my suggestion in regard to other clauses of the bill? If so, I feel highly honoured and I will make several suggestions.
What is his suggestion? Is it with regard to what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said?

I am suggesting that the minister explain why he puts *pickling onions in the exempted class so that they need not be sold by weight, while other onions have to be sold by weight. Why should pickling onions not be sold by weight?

As my hon. friend
knows, if you put larger onions into a small quart measure you could not get a true weight of them by measure. I mean to say a measure full of big onions would not weigh as much as if it were full of small ones. In regard to these things used regularly by the household, it is permissible to sell small onions by measure just as it is permissible to sell young green onions with the tops on and without having to weigh them. We can have these small onions sold by weight if my hon. friend wants it, but we want to try this out.

When this bill was
before the agriculture committee we were led to believe that in certain portions of the Dominion, more particularly the maritimes, and some of the eastern provinces, where they grew considerable quantities of potatoes, they

Root Vegetables Act
desired this legislation. But the view that was expressed in the committee by a number of members was that clause 3, which we are now considering, was altogether too drastic and far-reaching to suit conditions in many parts of Canada. It is true that in the committee the minister proposed an additional amendment to section 21 by which he might take care of a situation that was explained to him, but that amendment was very vague. It is true that it left in the hands of the minister power to meet a situation that might arise, but nothing definite was done to assure the committfee that that situation would be met. The situation will arise because clause 3 reads:
No person shall sell, offer, expose or have in possession for sale potatoes-
And then further on:
-unless such vegetables comply with all provisions of this' act and regulations made thereunder.
In our western country there are very few farmers who have not a few bushels of potatoes, twenty-five or fifty bushels, more or less, to dispose of in the spring of the year. They usually take them in to their local retail merchant and dispose of them there, or they may sell them to a neighbouring farmer. Under this legislation they would not dare to have such potatoes for sale unless they complied with all the provisions of this legislation. Just how far-reaching those provisions are going to be, remains to be seen, but some of them are outlined in clause 15 which states:
The governor in council may make regulations.
One of these is for the establishment of grades and another prescribes standard containers, and so on. Every farmer who has a few bushels of potatoes to sell must comply with all these regulations and everything that is laid down by the governor in council. If he does not comply with them, under clause 16 he is liable for the first offence to a fine not exceeding twenty-five dollars, for the second offence to a fine not exceeding fifty dollars, and for the third offence to a fine not exceeding two hundred dollars, and if he does not come through with the fine he is liable to a month's rest in gaol. I claim that this is altogether too drastic to apply in general to the whole of Canada. It may suit those districts where potatoes are grown in large quantities and where it would be worth while for the grower to comply with all these regulations, but it certainly is too drastic legislation to apply at least to that portion of the country in which I have the privilege of residing.

I would have the minister know that clause 3 is a new clause and not the reproduction of an old section. In addition to that he says that the unit of weight shall be a pound. The Weights and Measures Act, chapter 212, of the revised statutes of Canada, provides:
The unit or standard measure of capacity, from which all other measures of capacity, as well for liquids as for dry goods, shall be derived, shall be the gallon containing ten Dominion standard pounds weight of distilled water weighed in air against brass weights with the water and the air at the temperature of sixty-two degrees of Fahrenheit's thermometer, and with the barometer at thirty inches.
2.	The quart shall be one-fourth part of the
gallon.
3.	The pint shall be one-eighth part of the gallon.
4.	Two gallons shall be a peck.
5.	Eight gallons shall be a bushel.
That is the standard established by the Weights and Measures Act, but not only does the minister change the Weights and Measures Act, but clause 3 is a new clause despite what the minister has said three times in the committee. Clause 3 is not a reproduction of an old section. If the committee will turn to clause 12, it will find there the most serious clause of all. It reads:
Any inspector may detain for the time necessary to complete his inspection any shipment of vegetables in respect of which he has reasonable grounds for believing there is a violation of the act; such vegetables shall at all times be at the risk and charges of the owner thereof: and any inspector detaining vegetables shall give the owner, where ascertained, notice by prepaid telegram or letter that such vegetables are being detained in storage or otherwise, as the case may be.
I submit to the minister that he cannot hope that small market gardeners who have their vegetables gathered up by train, under the co-operative system in some cases, and brought into town, can comply with these regulations. If anybody is found in possession of one of these vegetables under clause 3, he is liable, and under clause 12 the inspector may take them and detain them until they are destroyed. He sends a telegram to the farmer who may be ten or twelve miles out in the country to tell him what he has done. Then the minister provides that the unit shall be, according to clause 4:
The standard pound avoirdupois shall be the unit of weight used.
We are now substituting a unit of weight, whereas heretofore under the Weights and Measures Act, chapter 212 of the revised statutes, the bushel was used. Now that measure as defined by the statute is no longer to be used with respect to dry goods and it
Root Vegetables Act

becomes an offence to sell by what, under the provisions of the statute, was heretofore the standard unit. Surely the minister does not mean that a small market gardener bringing his vegetables into town for sale is to be made a criminal by the law of parliament. It is an interference with the rights of the provinces under section 92 of the British North America Act. This parliament has the right to legislate with respect to exports, grading and things of that kind, and so far as that is concerned, the bill would be all right, but apart from all that, section 3 makes an entirely new offence, and section 12 gives one of the nine hundred inspectors which this Dominion is paying the right to seize these vegetables and deal with the offenders in the manner indicated by my hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). Surely my hon. friend the minister does not intend to deal with the matter in this way, and to ask this parliament to pass this form of legislation.	.

If my hon. friend
would take the bill section by section-
I am.

Of course, it is
necessary to refer to section 21 to know what the exemptions are, but if we are to start in the middle as well as at both ends, the matter will get tangled up in the minds of hon. gentlemen who have not studied this question. I would rather not deal with the question my hon. friend raises until we come to that particular section. I might say, however, that there is nothing in the world to hinder people from selling by the gallon, so long as there are seven and one-half pounds to the gallon, and as a matter of fact, they are selling by the gallon. So long as the weight is in the gallon, that is all right.

Would the minister say that the Prime Minister would have to have a special order in council passed to enable him to buy vegetables and fruits from his neighbours to keep his house going at Kingsmere?

I expect he will
have to comply with the law the same as other people.
We are on section 3, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

I would like to emphasize what has already been very well said by the hon. member for Kindersley regarding section

3, and I think the colleagues of my hon. friend the minister ought to take serious note of this. Section 3 says:
No person shall sell, offer, expose, or have in possession for sale potatoes, onions, turnips, artichokes, beets, carrots, parsnips or such other vegetables as may be named in this act or by the governor in council under the provisions of this act unless such vegetables comply with all provisions of this act and regulations made thereunder.
I appeal to the Prime Minister for a moment. Here we have a section that says that a small farmer in any section of Canada- I will bring it right home to mf own district in a moment-must be thoroughly versed in this act and in any regulations that may be made under this act by the governor in council. Some of us have had years of experience in this house, and yet I venture to say that there is not a member of this house to-day, be he agriculturist, farmer, or following any other occupation, who has the faintest idea, or anything but the remotest idea, of the regulations now in existence under this act.

We have
all violated the act.

I venture to say that the regulations are to-day being violated, not maliciously, but simply because they are not known.
I turn now, if the minister will pardon me. to the explanatory note on section. 15, which provides that proceedings to recover penalties for violation of any of the regulations passed under this act may be taken under Part XV of the criminal code. Let us be sensible and ask ourselves this question: Are we going to expose all the small farmers of this country, as well as the big producers of potatoes and vegetables, to prosecution under the criminal code if they fail to observe the intricate provisions of this act?
Let me analyse the section now, and apply it to a business that I know, that of the small farmer in British Columbia. We have there hundreds of farmers, who raise from five to ten acres of potatoes, and possibly have half an acre of onions, a few carrots and beets, and so on, and they sell them in the locality to a sawmill and small industries of that kind I have in mind a farm of about sixty acres, where they raise about ten acres of potatoes, a few hogs, some apples, and general farm produce, most of which is sold to a little village close beside the farm, where there is a sawmill and other very small industrial works. The employees buy this farmer's produce, and let me say to the minister that that is the finest customer a small farmer can have, the very best. In many instances these people, know-

Root Vegetables Act
ing what the various farmers in the neighbourhood produce, drive out to the farm in a Ford car or some other vehicle and buy a substantial portion of his produce. Now section 3 provides:
No person shall sell, offer, expose, or have in possession for sale potatoes, onions, turnips, artichokes, beets, carrots, parsnips or such other vegetables as may be named in this act or by the governor in council under the provisions of this act unless such vegetables comply with all provisions of this act and regulations made thereunder.
That is, these vegetables must be sorted, graded to size, weighed out in bags which must contain a certain amount, and all such stuff as that, and another section provides that the weight must be marked on the face of the container. Now in British Columbia these potatoes are put in gunny sacks; that is the jute sack, the usual standard sack. The sack is used for grain in the first place, and after it has been used once or twice for that purpose, it is sold second-hand to farmers such as I have mentioned, who buy it cheaply, and use it for sacking their potatoes, carrots, turnips and such like. These sacks when well filled and properly sewn will hold about one hundred pounds, and generally speaking these potatoes are sold by weight. If a carload is being sold, the potatoes are sacked, and the sacks are weighed on scales, and they try to put one hundred pounds in a sack, and the carload is sold by weight, and usually the transaction is very satisfactorily arranged between buyer and seller.
That is what we are aiming at. Mark the weight on the bag.

Let me continue my point for a moment. We have large growers, as well as these small farmers to whom I have referred. We have large growers in the Ashcroft district, around Ashcroft and Kamloops, who are raising potatoes by the hundreds of acres and who sell them by the carload, put up in sacks. They are sold to the wholesaler in the city by the carload, in sacks, and he puts them in his warehouse, and then sells them to the grocer in the city, in sacks, and the grocer dumps them in his cellar or puts them into his bins and sells them either by the sack, the half sack, or by the pound. Now, I submit that by this section you are imposing on the small producer an obligation that is absolutely beyond his capacity to perform, that is the point. I say it is beyond his capacity to observe this regulation.
As my hon. leader said a moment ago, if it is a question of the form in which potatoes shall be exported from this country, that is a different matter. It may be desirable to
say that when potatoes are exported to the European market or some other foreign market, they shall be crated, graded, and so on.
I am willing to say that that is open to reasonable discussion, but in that case they are sold not by the carload, not by the ton, but by the cargo. I appeal to the Prime Minister that this section 3 should not become a statute law of this country. I again draw attention to it. It says:
No person shall sell, offer, expose, or have in possession for sale potatoes, onions, turnips, artichokes, beets, carrots, parsnips or _ such other vegetables as may be named in this act or by the governor in council under the provisions of this act unless such _ vegetables comply with all provisions of this act and regulations made thereunder.
I say it is not fair for us to pass this legislation; it is not wise for us to do so, apart altogether from the constitutional point of' view. It is not fair to lay this burden on the ordinary producer of this country. It is a burden that is absolutely beyond the capacity of the small producer, who is trying to make a living by raising small quantities of vegetables. The average small farmer in British Columbia gets his returns from potatoes, apples and pears, small fruits, such as strawberries, raspberries, loganberries and plums, honey, eggs and butter and milk. That is the most desirable type of farmer you could have for British Columbia. You cannot ask a man like that to be an expert on the intricacies of regulations governing every branch of his business; the poor fellow would be literally driven mad.

Does the hon.
member appeal for the removal of all sorts of regulations regarding grading of vegetables for the local market?

I would certainly argue
for the minimizing to the lowest possible point of the regulations that interfere with the activities of this class of farmers.

We have power to
do that under the act.

That is just the point.
It seems to me that what the minister does is this, he starts in with the maximum weight of regulations and interference and then grades it down. I want to see our statutes imposing the minimum interference in business and trade. Section 14 reads:
An inspection certificate signed by an inspector or any person charged with the enforcement of this act or regulations made thereunder, shall be prima facie evidence of the truth of the statements contained therein.

And customs inspectors.
He has nine hundred in his department.

I appeal to the Prime
Minister on this larger and broader question, that every inspection increases the cost of production of the article inspected. You cannot escape it, for it is an economic truth. It is obvious that someone must pay the cost. Every time you appoint an inspector at a thousand or two thousand dollars a year, give him a car and buy his gasoline, and all the rest of it, someone is paying for that expense. Who? You can apply it at any stage you like, but it must come on the cost of production somewhere.
And the cost of living generally.

Undoubtedly. This is a
serious matter. This morning a young gentleman who has made a study of politico-economic questions intimated to me that one out of every five of the male adults of Canada is employed in some form of government position-federal, provincial, municipal. If that is true, and he assured me it was, then it shows the burden that is being placed upon the shoulders of the people, because you cannot call those officials producers. Indirectly they may classify themselves as such, but they are a part of the cost of administration. This is an overhead charge on everything that goes on in the country. So I say we ought to be very careful about increasing the cost of this class of business to the farmers of Canada.

I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister withdraw section 3, not because I think there is any harm in it, but because it does not mean anything. It is a superfluity. It is only a reiteration of the general law which says, you must comply with this act. Section 16 provides a penalty for those who violate any section of the act. You cannot get any other meaning out

of section 3 than that, and if it is obnoxious to hon. members I suggest that it be withdrawn. I do not know why all this opposition is raised to section 4, because the principle has been in effect for several years at least.
It has not been enforced.

No, they pass these drastic
laws and often do not enforce them. What was the law?
All potatoes, onions, artichokes, beets, carrots, parsnips and turnips offered for sale shall be sold by weight, and the standard pound avoirdupois shall be the unit of weight used.
So after all we are not doing anything worse than we did last time this act was revised, and I do not remember any objection raised to the section at that time. I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in regard to section 14, that it makes the certificate of the inspector superior to the law of evidence. I also agree with what he said as to section 12, that an inspector may practically ruin a small man against whom he has a grudge, by holding up his stuff while he deliberates upon it; which is quite unnecessary because the stuff is either right or wrong, and this is easily ascertained.
After all, the main principle of the act is that we should sell potatoes by the pound, and I am quite sure that that is acceptable to the average farmer in British Columbia. How else would he sell them? We put up our potatoes, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre knows, in 100-pound sacks, and the sale being by weight, fraud is prevented. If she buys by the sack, how is the housekeeper to know whether she is getting ninety pounds or a hundred pounds? I remember once trying to sell some potatoes to a storekeeper. I asked for a certain price in 100-pound bags, twenty to the ton. On my declining his offer of a lower price, he said, "I will give you so much more if you will put them up in 95-pound sacks, and then I can sell them for 100-pound sacks." I do not think there is any harm in carrying out this principle of selling by weight. We are doing it already.

I might point out that it is the practice of the draftsman of the Justice department whenever they make a change in a section to repeat the whole section in order to simplify matters. Previously the law applied only to potatoes and onions, and it worked out so admirably that we decided to make it apply to all vegetables.

Section 3 is entirely new.

Therefore the principle of this legislation has been in force for five years and has been found to be sound. There has never been any occasion for alarm
or confusion in applying that principle.
Not the principle embodied in section 3.

The same principle is involved. I think my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre enunciated a very sound principle, that when enacting such legislation it is well to start with the minimum of restrictions and regulations. That is exactly ' what we did five years ago. We started with a small specific number of vegetables which were recognized on almost every market. There was no doubt that those vegetables- potatoes and onions and so forth-should be sold by weight, and that was done. That having worked out satisfactorily we extended the principle to others. I cannot understand what the difficulty is about. I remember when we enacted the egg regulations we took the opposite attitude; that is to say, we made a very wide exemption in favour of poultry-men and farmers generally. These regulations did not apply to farmers marketing fifteen dozen or under in one day. This provision has worked out satisfactorily in a sense, but gradually it has come to be grossly abused. You may sell fifteen dozen as many times in one day as you like, and if only you are persistent enough you may defy the law. This exemption in the case of eggs was provided with the best intentions, but it has grown into a decided abuse. Nevertheless exemptions are necessary at the beginning, and that is one reason why we have taken the power either to reduce the exemptions, under section 21, or to increase them to meet the requirements as they arise, thus obviating the necessity of coming to parliament so frequently. That is the purpose, but there is no new principle involved.
What new principle is involved in section 3 which is not covered by section 16?

We are including
a lot of new vegetables.

Section 16 provides that
every person who by himself or through the agency of another person violates any of the provisions of the act shall be liable. Is not that all-inclusive? What is there in section 3 which is not covered under that section?

I understand that
the Justice department, to make it perfectly airtight, advised this section.
Isn't that my point? You are providing the maximum to start with in order to make it airtight.
We have been operating for five years under the minimum, and some people have been able to get past us in the courts.
How many thousand inspectors will the minister require under this act, and by whom will they be paid?

We shall have a few less than we ought to have, but if my hon. friend will look up the estimates of the department the year before this government came into power he will find that we are exceeding the number for the first time this year.

I am not interested in that;
I desire to know how many inspectors there will be.
If we are extravagant in the number of inspectors we have we must be very economical in our management, or the aggregate estimates would be larger than they are.

How many inspectors will
be needed?
I do not know how many. Some of the inspectors perform duties under as many as five acts.

How many do you require
in Montreal, for example?

When we are on
the estimates I shall be delighted to give that information; I am not prepared to say offhand. My deputy informs me that in the city of Montreal we have three.

"Or such other vegetables as may be named by the governor in council".

Yes; in other
words, he is not changing the act. The minister is asking us to give the governor in council power to make any changes that may be thought necessary, and I object to that most decidedly. Later on I shall have something to say in that regard, because if orders in council are to be passed under this act it will only make it worse for the poor unfortunate farmer. It has been well pointed out that it would be impossible for the small farmer to keep this law. Certainly it will be very difficult indeed for him to know what the law is if orders in council are to be passed including other vegetables. The ordinary farmer in my county does not take the Canada Gazette, and even if the orders in council were published therein, I do not think he would know about them. I have looked over this bill rather carefully and it seems to be the new sections which the minister wants to get through. Every one of these new sections is objectionable, and I can see no argument whatever for section 3. As has been pointed out, there is no use in passing legislation which cannot possibly be complied with, and it is utterly impossible to imagine that the small farmers and dealers in this country could comply with section 3. So that the minister is beginning by making criminals out of these farmers right away. Other sections have been commented upon, and it seems to me that the minister wants to get more inspectors in his department, and that this is the main reason for his bringing his bill before us. Now, there is a feeling in the country'
Why should I want more inspectors?

Section 10 gives the minister power to appoint an advisory board which may at his request prepare and recommend standards and grades, and so forth. Then he may appoint "such inspectors and other officers as are deemed necessary." This is a new section. There is a feeling in the country, I say, that the minister has too many inspectors already. I have asked my hon. friends many times to name one or two or any number of inspectors that are unnecessary, and I shall be delighted to dispense with their services.
Why does the minister want to have section 10 enacted empowering him to appoint more inspectors?

Does the minister mean that he has already appointed inspectors without authority? Is that what he means?

In other words, this act does not apply to vegetables other than those covered by the old act, but by passing this new act we will place many of our small dealers and farmers under a law which they cannot possibly understand. Power is given under section 10 to appoint an advisory board and such other officers as are deemed necessary, and under sections 12 and 14 the inspectors are given more and more power over these people. The smaller dealers in this country will be afraid bo carry on their ordinary business as they have been carrying it on in the past. Apparently these are the sections which the minister desires most, because there are no vegetables mentioned other than those which are already included in the present act.

I would point out again what was freely discussed in the agricultural committee, that there might be some injustice to farmers selling in small lots. It was my suggestion that, we should have power to step in and make regulations exempting farmers from these provisions if we found any injustice being done. Why not do it now?

We do not want to anticipate trouble. We have given these wide exemptions in connection with the sale of eggs, and I am sure no one in British Columbia wants that exemption of 15 dozen freed from the regulations, as it is now. How will this work out in the New Westminster market, for example? I understand the minister has been there and has seen the farmers bring in their goods, which they sell to the citizens of the town and district. In that market so far as I know there is very little selling by weight; vegetables are mostly sold in packages, in boxes, in sacks and so on. It seems to me there would be great consternation in New Westminster and other markets if this law were put into effect; it would be a great inconvenience to the farmers and to the purchasers, who are accustomed to buy their goods in boxes or parcels. More than that, it seems to me that the minister is badly twisted with regard to potatoes. As I read the proposed act, it will be lawful to sell new potatoes otherwise than by weight, but old potatoes must' be sold by weight. That is directly opposite to the custom which now prevails at least in British Columbia, ordinary potatoes are sold in sacks or by the bushel, while new potatoes are always sold by weight. I doubt very much whether under section 21 new potatoes can be sold otherwise than by weight except when they are shipped, because the minister will notice that section 21 says:
(a) to new potatoes when shipped between the 1st day of July and the 30th day of September	
What about new potatoes which are sold on the market but which have not been shipped? How will this affect potatoes which are sold direct by the producer to the consumer? They are brought in to the market by the farmer, and unless you have some extraordinary interpretation of the word " shipped," I do not see that they can be sold except by weight.

My non. friend has asked me how these regulations will apply to New Westminster and other small markets. Most of these regulations will apply just as they are being applied at present. These vegetables are sold now by weight, so there will be no great change there. With regard to subsection (a) of section 21, only one word is underlined, which shows that that' subsection was in the act previously, and we managed to survive under it. I would ask the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), as a practical vegetable grower, coming from a district where this business is carried on extensively, if he would like to make these exemptions wider. I remember we discussed this in the committee and it was thought that if we exempted all farmers it would allow persons who were both traders and farmers to come under the exemptions, so it was thought better to assume the authority to widen these exemptions, and if injustices were caused we could meet the situation by the necessary changes. As a matter of fact, in the Seeds Act we have specifically exempted farmers dealing with one another, and we have done the same in connection with artificial fertilizer. We could make these exemptions so wide that all farmers would not come under the provisions of the act in their dealings with each other, but if we did that it was thought that men who were both dealers and traders as well as growers would be exempt from the provisions of this law, which would not be wise. We have taken the, power to meet conditions as they arise, and since most of these troubles have not arisen during the last five years I do not think we should anticipate them and legislate for them in advance.

I suggest to the minister

So that I think hon. members will readily see that there is no intention on the part of the department or of the minister to apply this act to the small dealings of neighbours among themselves, or between persons within the same community.
It says so, though.

Now I want to explain to the committee some of the benefits that have accrued from this act to our growers and to our dealers in the maritime provinces in regard to the shipment of potatoes.
That is export business.
It is interprovincial trade.
Exactly.

And also trade
within the provinces themselves. So far as it has been applied it has not been compulsory except where requested by the shippers or growers. Many of our wholesale dealers two years ago asked that the act be put into force
so that inspectors would be supplied by the department for the grading of carloads of potatoes when a request to that effect was made. That action was taken by the department a year ago last September and many inspectors were specially appointed for the enforcement of this act in Prince Edward Island. A per carload fee of $5 a car was placed upon inspection, and those who got the benefit of the inspection paid the cost of it. When the dealers buy potatoes from the farmers they buy Canada A stock, and if on inspection at the car door they prove to be below standard the farmer has to regrade his stock. These potatoes are sold to dealers in Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa and other of the large markets in central Canada, according to the grade, the greater proportion of them being sold as Canada A grade. When they arrive at destination the bill of lading is accompanied by a certificate signed by the inspector stating that he inspected those potatoes and that they are up to the grade specified in the certificate. If the man who buys the potatoes feels that they do not turn out right, he immediately telegraphs to the man he buys from, who arranges with the department to have an inspector sent to inspect the car at point of destination before it is unloaded. If the potatoes are found to come up to the grade specified in the certificate, then the man who sold the potatoes can collect his price for the shipment. If the potatoes were sold without the inspector's certificate and objection was taken at point of destination to the quality, the grower or seller, would have no recourse except to accept the word of the man who bought the potatoes. If the deal took place on a falling market, nine times out of ten the man who shipped the potatoes would lose very heavily on account of not being in a position to protect himself against any complaint that might be made regarding his shipment. It can be seen from the market reports covering the last two years that the price of potatoes of Canada A grade from the maritimes has advanced. Inspected stock from the east sells at from ten to fifteen cents a bag more in the central markets of Canada than potatoes that come in without inspection from other points.
The request that has come forward from our people for changes in the grades has helped to bring about the changes in the act. The Department of Agriculture and the Department of Justice can explain better than those of us who are engaged in the actual

That will be covered in this legislation by regulation.
How are the general public going to know?
