The hon. gentleman did
not catch my question, which is after all largely the quarrel with this legislation as it is drafted. Let us leave out of account the man who ships from one end of the province to the other or to any point a long distance away. Let us take the case of the farmer- and there are tens of thousands of them in Canada-who sells his products in his little village or town to a sawmill or pulp mill close by, which by the way is his best customer. Does the hon. gentleman think it is fair to apply to such dealings the same regulations that he would apply to the larger transactions to which he has referred?

Root Vegetables Act

I do not see
my ton. friend's point in asking whether it is fair. If a man wants to sell to his neighbour Canada A potatoes, his neighbour has a right to expect that he will deliver Canada A potatoes.

I agree, but that is not
the point.
To that extent the act is enforced.
Who is to determine when the act is to be enforced and when it is not to be enforced? Surely if we pass an act at all it ought to be enforced.

The regulations will determine that. The objection may be raised that we are doing by regulation and order in council what should be done by legislation, but it has been found necessary to define grades by regulations rather than by the statute.

But the legislation, if we
accept it, states:
No person-
That is, no farmer, no dealer, no grower.
-shall sell, offer, expose, or have in possession for sale potatoes .... unless such vegetables comply with all provisions of this act and regulations made thereunder.

It says, "all
provisions of this act and regulations made thereunder." If my hon. friend follows that out, he will find that it is within the right and power of the minister and the department, upon the advice of the advisory board, to make reasonable regulations to protect both the seller and the buyer from dishonest and disreputable dealings in the trade, and it has had that effect, particularly in regard to potatoes, I do not see why it should not be extended to other vegetables where practicable.

The hon. member
for Comox-Alberni has suggested that one of these sections could be dispensed with. I would like to have an opportunity of discussing the matter with the Justice department, to see what can be done without weakening the bill. We have had a full discussion, and I suggest that these two sections stand in the meantime, so that we may see what amendments can be made that will not sacrifice the intent of the bill. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni made a similar suggestion in regard to the Seed Grain Act; we brought down an amendment accordingly, and it went through immediately.

Might I suggest
another matter that might be referred to the Justice department? In the act there are very clear definitions of "minister" "inspectors", "vegetables", "grade" and "container", but in section 3 there appears the word "person", and there is no definition of that word. It seems to me it ought to be made very clear whether the word applies to women as well as to men.

The Interpretation Act
covers that. There is another difficulty that I would like to mention to the minister. This statute in terms repeals an act that came into force in Canada on the first of February last, being chapter 181 of the revised statutes of Canada. That statute defined in terms the grades of potatoes, onions, and so forth. The new statute does not define them in terms, but it creates an advisory board. It does not say how many there shall be on that board, and there is no indication as to how they shall be selected, or where they shall come from.
We can insert that.

I am pointing out what
it means. It also provides that they may report to the minister, but it is the governor in council that passes the regulations. Now the whole question of grading, which heretofore in Canada was dealt with by the statute which is now to be repealed, is to be left to regulations about which the average man can know little, and his opportunities for getting knowledge of them will be less. He must depend largely upon the Canada Gazette, whereas heretofore he had chapter 181 of the revised statutes of Canada from which he could obtain all the information that he required with respect to potatoes, onions, and other vegetables. I go a step further, and this is a question which I wduld ask the minister to consider very carefully apart from what has been said by others. Section 15 says that the governor in council may make regulations:
To prescribe the time when any regulation shall come into operation, the particular kind or kinds of vegetables to which it shall apply, and the part or parts of Canada within which it shall be in force.
That means different grades for different parts of Canada, depending upon the political pressure that may be put on the minister or the government. That is what that means, and that is why it should not be placed upon the statute book. Heretofore we have had a standard grade, one grade throughout the country fixed by statute. We are now leaving it in the hands of the governor in council to make regulations with respect to many

Root Vegetables Act

things, including among other grades-one for one part of Canada, another for another-the very thing that should not be if the statute is to be constitutional, for it is quite clear that if the statute is to have any validity as a statute, it must deal with either foreign trade or interprovincial trade. If it deals with purely local matters within the province, the province has the power, and not the Dominion. It is only because the Dominion's legislation operates throughout the country as a whole, dealing either with interprovincial or export trade, that this parliament can deal with the matter. Here we are asked to give the governor in council power to make different grades applicable to different parts of the country. Surely the minister does not intend that. That is the very thing that chapter 181 says should not be done, because the desire is to have some sort of uniform legislation throughout the country.
In addition, this means an increase in the number of inspectors, and it clothes them with enormous power. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, in answer to a question that I directed to him, pointed out, it allows the certificate of an inspector to be prim a facie evidence of the commission of an offence. Just imagine itl The certificate of an inspector, with the regulations in his hands, not published, is to be prima facie evidence of guilt before a justice of the peace. I ask the minister if he thinks that can be tolerated in Canada. I leave it to the minister, does he think that sort of legislation, in this country at any rate, should be given support and approval, and especially in view of the fact that there is the statute already defining grades and providing for sales by weight, without the necessity of making any new provision? There you have chapter 181 of the revised statutes of Canada, and now we are going to take all that power out of the hands of parliament and put it into the hands of an advisory board, not knowing how it is to be selected or appointed. The governor in council may make regulations applicable to Alberta, perhaps, and not to Saskatchewan, applicable to British Columbia, and not to Ontario, and the certificate of the inspector is to be prime facia evidence of violation of the provisions of this act. Surely the minister does not want to do that.

Most of the hon.
gentleman's remarks have been based on the assumption that the law provides for only one grade of any article to be applicable throughout Canada.
No.

My hon. friend
surely knows that we have two grain inspection districts in Canada, and have had for forty years.
The old act, the Manitoba Grain Act, was changed to the Canada Grain Act.
The western standards do not apply to eastern Canada.

The act is an act for
the whole of Canada, but with respect to certain standards, of course, they do not grow the same kind of grain in the east as in the west.

But the western
standards do not apply to eastern Canada.
They cannot.

So there is no
precedent being created here at all. As a matter of fact, in the Fruit Act as it was, the apples of British Columbia were compulsorily graded for export, and to-day they are not compulsorily graded for the maritimes, and that has been approved by the Justice department.

I am not speaking of
apples. Chapter 181 is an act to regulate the sale and inspection of root vegetables, and this bill seeks to repeal that statute. Section 3 of chapter 181 defines the following grades of potatoes: (a) Canada A quality; (b) Canada B quality; (c) Canada C ungraded quality. That is what I am pointing out, the variations.

What is the use of grading two varieties of vegetables by statute, and leaving all the rest to be done by order in council? We are simply treating them all alike; that is all. My hon. friend laughs at that. We have graded potatoes and onions before. Why from now on should we have potatoes and onions graded by statute, and all the other vegetables graded by order in council ?
The minister from Prince Edward Island told us that the grading of potatoes has worked out well. Now the Minister of Agriculture proposes to change it.

We are not changing it. Every now and then my hon. friend starts off on a new tack and under a wrong assumption as to facts. He has made two or three statements about grading contrary to the statute, when half of our grain this year was graded by the grain standard board.

Root Vegetables Act
We are not talking about grain; we are dealing with roots and vegetables.
This is a precedent' -something that is very dear to the lawyer's mind. I think we might let sections 3 and 4 stand, and go ahead with the rest of the bill.
Withdraw the whole bill.

I see no reason
why we cannot get some relaxation of this section as suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) without sacrificing its strength.

We are stressing
potatoes and grain.
The same principle is involved. Grading is grading, whether it be wheat or anything else.

What is in the
minister's mind with regard to inspection of these smaller vegetables? We go to the market here in Ottawa and see displayed for sale bunches of carrots and other vegetables. How are they to be inspected? How is the purchaser to know that they have been inspected?

Our inspectors go
on the various markets of Canada, where there is a substantial business, including Toronto and Ottawa, and draw attention to any violation of the law, and if that violation is persisted in we prosecute.

You will need all
the adult population in Canada to enforce this section. For instance, are you going to have an inspector in Aylmer to inspect the farmer's
little truck load of vegetables?
We have graded for home consumption a changeable article like eggs, ten times as difficult to administer as the grading of vegetables, and yet the public have accepted that as a good law.

And it has been held
[DOT] ultra vires by the courts.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at six it had been agreed to let sections 3 and 4 stand. Sections 1 and 2 had passed. The committee is now considering section 5. Shall the section carry?

So far as export conditions are concerned the minister is on pretty safe ground. Personally I think it would be a good thing for everyone on this side of the house if this bill went through as introduced to-day. I am rather inclined to think that the minister has not very well read the lessons of history regarding restrictive legislation. I remember some time ago, when the party which I have the honour and pleasure to support was in power, we imposed restrictions on the carrying of arms; we made everyone having in his possession a rifle or shotgun take out a permit. It affected about 99 persons out of every 100 in my riding and created a particular hell for everyone who had supported that legislation. As regards restrictive legislation of this nature, dealing with the domestic business of our farmers, I think the minister is on dangerous ground if he is looking to the peace, comfort and welfare of his government. This legislation will be obnoxious to the people, and the result will be only one of two things: either the spirit of the law will not be observed at all, or the act will create a lot of trouble for the minister and his government. That would of course be reflected more or less on every man who is in parliament to-day, because the people would be coming to us with all their grievances, as they have done in the past, using rather harsh language towards the government and those in authority as well as towards everyone else associated with the act.
I have on a great many occasions in this house objected to all these restrictions that are being put on the liberties of the people. It seems to me that it is becoming a fad; we are almost going crazy in this regard. And this is just another piece of such legislation which the minister is bringing in. The act will never be enforced in the smaller places; I think I am quite safe in saying that. You could not enforce it. It will only create intense dissatisfaction; it will provide more positions to be filled and will incur more expense. It will indirectly run up the cost of living and the cost of doing business. I think the minister would be well advised to abandon it so far as the domestic field is concerned As regards the interprovincial trade, the min-
56103-145i
Root Vegetables Act

ister this afternoon had, I thought, some regard to this phase of the question. But if you are going to apply this legislation to all the little trading transactions that take place on the country roads, in the villages and towns, and render the farmers liable to the penalties -peeified in the act, you will only create 'rouble. The act will be a farce and will *'.ever be enforced; if you try to enforce it- well, God help the government and the people who try to carry it out.

I assume that my hon. friend's remarks apply to section 5, the one under discussion. I may say that every vegetable grower in Canada in every province has asked for this section. At least one representative from New Brunswick in this house has urged upon me the necessity for it, in order to provide for compulsory inspection if we deem it desirable to take that power, and the grading of vegetables for export. It is the same as in regard to cheese and butter; there is no new principle involved. The fact is, we are being urged to pass this legislation
For export, yes.
From what quarters has the minister been requested to bring in this legislation?

The representatives of the vegetable growers have requested it. If my hon. friend wishes me to mention names, I may say that one gentleman who has urged it upon me is the newest member from New Brunswick. One of the reasons why they want this legislation is the fact that their market in Cuba was nearly ruined by the export of defective potatoes to that country. The representative of Cuba-with whom I happen to be living-has told me that unless something is done to improve the New Brunswick potato situation his country will have to exclude those potatoes from the Cuban market; not that the potatoes are not good; but they are very carelessly handled. In order to satisfy myself I got a barrel of these potatoes shipped to the fruit commissioner's office and, accompanied by Mr. Caldwell, who was a member of this house, two years or so ago, I went and inspected this sample. I found from 30 to 40 per cent of the potatoes defective; they were cracked or wounded or bruised in some way. And they were all beautiful potatoes. But after travelling a considerable distance, broken and cracked, and passing through the warmer climate of the southern Atlantic, a great many of them were on the point of heating and it was just a question whether they should not be dumped into the sea. The result was that we were

given warning that, unless this condition stopped, the Cuban people would have to put an embargo on our potatoes. It was due, not to the farmers, but to the dealers in New Brunswick who were handling these potatoes. In compliance with an urgent request from every part of the Dominion, we are taking some power with regard to the export of potatoes, just as we do in regard to anything else that is shipped out. These powers may appear to be far-reaching and. to some, exasperating. But I may assure the committee that we are not beginning to take in respect of these matters anything like the power which is exercised in Australia and New Zealand. There the authorities go very much further than we do, and say to a man that.unless his goods are up to a certain standard they shall not be exported at all to any countiy, because Australian and New Zealand growers do not want their reputation injured abroad. We exclude no farm product from export which is at all edible, but we want it graded just as we do with butter,, cheese, eggs and many other articles to which I have referred. Then it must be remembered that we are only asking for authority to do it; it may be a year before we bring it into practice. We were grading fruit for export two years before we applied the law for home consumption. When the people become familiar with a law by using it voluntarily, we gradually make it compulsory when we are asked to do so.

I hope the minister did not misunderstand me; I think he is absolutely right so far as export business is concerned, but I believe he is absolutely wrong when he tries to apply it to all the little domestic transactions which take place in the small towns. For my own sake politically I hope he goes through with it; this bill will give me a lot of votes. But I am trying to do a favour for the government by keeping the minister right, and at the same time I am trying to keep peace among the farmers in my riding.

I have agreed to let these two sections stand. This is not an arbitrary measure; I am told that this bill is the result of requests from growers, shippers, consumers, and the trade generally. If one of the Toronto members who is a prominent wholesale produce dealer were here, he would tell you that these provisions are necessary; in the committee he confirmed them all. I am sure the growers, as represented by the hon. member for Yale, are also unanimous in their support of these provisions. However, the two sections to which my hon. friend is

Root Vegetables Act
referring will stand, and probably we can find some less provocative language which at the same time will attain the desired end. I should like to consult the Department of Justice before changing the wording, because they have said that this is the correct form.
I have a good deal of respect for the ability of the minister.

I do not rise as an authority on farming, but I would like to say a word or two in general on this bill. I apologize for speaking on it at all, because as I have already said I do not know very much about farming, although a large section of my constituency is composed of farming communities. At that, I am not worse than most of the other members who spoke this afternoon; I presume a good many of them in these days of the automobile are like myself, hardly able to tell a horse from a cow. However, coming as I do from a section of northern Ontario where farming is a very difficult pioneering occupation for a great many people, I do not like to see too many restrictions placed upon farmers. Perhaps one third of my constituency is composed of people w'ho are pioneer farmers, who have gone into bush country similar to that of northern Quebec and some parts of British Columbia, and who have had to hew their homes out of the bush. In many cases they have been confronted with many difficulties, and I do not like to see more restrictions placed upon those men who already have enough difficulty in making a living. It is very difficult to populate that section of Ontario extending west from North Bay to the Manitoba boundary, an area almost as large as Germany and France together. It will supply a large area of magnificent farming land once it is cleared, but it requires a long, hard life of pioneering in most cases before enough land is cleared to make good homes for the farmers. In view of that, and in view of the fact that these farmers sell practically all their vegetables in the towns and cities of the neighbourhood, I do not like to see their difficulties increased in any way. As a matter of fact, I have the impression that we are too prone to legislation in our country; perhaps it would be -a good thing if we had a closed season for legislation extending from about January 1 to July 1. That would pretty well cover the session of Parliament, and would result in a shorter and more profitable session while letting the country go along in better shape than is now the case.

It would give US' a more
contented community.

As the hon. member (Mr. Cahan) has suggested, probably it would give us a more contented community. Unfortunately in our country there are a great many people who believe that because something is old it is of no use and that only the new is useful. They read of something which has been done in New Zealand or in some other country or state and think we must immediately copy it. I do not believe that is necessary in all cases. I think we might well leave these restrictive bills out of our legislation for a while and let our pioneering sections grow up and get further advanced before such measures are passed. Most of the people are not familiar with this sort of thing, and they will not take the trouble to read them.
I am speaking very generally now, because I quite understand that in regard to exports of fruit, wheat and many other agricultural products it is necessary for the good name of Canada that we have grades. I do not question that for a moment, but at the same time I am not one of those who believe that the ordinary buyer in the small town or city, or even in the large town or city, cannot look after himself or herself pretty well. We have in my city a market to which the farmers of the surrounding district come two or three times a week, and they get along very well with the people m the town. Unfortunately for the farmers in that pioneering section, during the war the government of which I was a supporter advocated greater production. I say unfortunately, because greater production meant that all kinds of people in the towns and cities produced fruits and vegetables in their back yards or in vacant lots. That became something of an obsession with many people, and as a result the farmers in that section of the country find it very difficult to make a living. We are finding it very hard to keep people on the land, and I believe restrictive legislation of this kind has something to do with driving the people off the farms because it makes things more difficult for them. I suggest to the minister, with the best intentions in the world, that in the future we might well drop some of this restrictive legislation, particularly as it affects truck farmers. I will admit readily that for export on a large scale, in order to compete in the markets of the world, it is necessary that we should have grades in order to give our products a good name, but I think we might easily go too far in other directions. I say this with no intended reflection upon the civil servants in the department of my hoc
Root Vegetables Act

friend, but I think unfortunately it is true that there are a number of civil servants in every branch of public life who look around for wavs in which to use their energies.
Oh, no.

I have had something to do with inspectors of various kinds in various branches of governmental work, and I have found that with the best intentions in the world, and meaning nothing wrong, they are often looking for something to restrict. They desire an opportunity to put their names on legislation; they like to point out that they were the fathers of this or that measure. I believe we might check that tendency in all branches of the public service and leave our people in quiet and contentment for a while. That will give our pioneer sections an opportunity to fill up with farmers, who will have time to get established on the land without too many restrictions. The people in the towns and cities have things a great deal easier than these pioneer farmers, so I say they should be allowed to take a chance once in a while. It is the old story; if you put a support on a healthy child's back the back will never get strong, and the same thing applies to the people in our towns and citites. Let them take a chance; they are pretty good gamblers now, as anyone can see by watching the stock markets. Let them gamble with the farmers of their communities, and in that way the farmers will have a chance to get well established on the land, especially in those sections of northern Ontario to which I have referred.

I wonder if my
hon. friend would take his own prescription when applied to the many inspections which take place at Fort William and Port Arthur. Why harass the farmers, he might well say, with all this inspectional service, not letting them pass with a single grain of wheat, oats or barley without some monster inspector wanting to do something to make himself officious and to degrade his grain for him? Would that be good for Canada, or would it hurt Canada in the grain markets of the world?

The minister has taken
up a subject in regard to which I admitted he is correct. I was not referring to that. I admitted the need in exports of importance.

If it is good for
the goose it is good for the gander.

I am not so sure.
i Mr. Manion.]

Which is the goose and
which is the gander?

We have made
exceptions. There are exceptions in connection with the grain trade. You can send forward mixed cargoes as long as you indicate on them that they are. mixed. So there are exceptions in this legislation and there is power to make dozens of exceptions if we find in the administration that exceptions are necessary. But why discuss that phase of it? I want to make some progress. The domestic side of the question is embodied in clauses 3 and 4, and nobody is objecting to clause 5. Even going as far as we are in clause 5 we are not within approaching distance of what the other overseas dominions are doing in protecting the quality of their goods in sending them overseas for export. We are miles behind them.

I am
not going to discuss the bill in general, but I want -to point out to the minister again that the matter will be materially helped as regards the chief objections that have been taken by changing the word "person" in the different clauses. In clause 3, which was allowed to stand, the second word in the first line is "person" and the same word appears in clause 6, 7, 8, 9 and so on. The discussion for the last hour or so has been in regard to the export end of the vegetable business. That does not cover the thousands of farmers who wish to trade between themselves. Throughout western Canada and in some of the other provinces one farmer will call up his neighbour and want to know if he has a few potatoes or something else and that neighbour will throw three or four sacks in his car and take them over.
Does my hon. friend object to grading vegetables for export?
No.

That is what we
are dealing with.

Why
apply it to the individual who is not exporting? That is my point and that is the point which was raised by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) and received favourably by the minister. The word "person" appears all through the clause. Why not substitute the word " dealer"?

The custom right
along has been to provide by regulation for grading for export. There may be a better way but I do not know what it is. If any-

Root Vegetables Act
body will evolve a better way I shall be delighted to accept it because we want nothing but the best. We cannot put all these details into the law. There is scarcely any law, especially affecting agriculture, which has not a provision for making regulations based upon the law so that changes can be made rapidly from time to time as the circumstances warrant, instead of our having to wait until parliament meets to get an obvious injustice corrected.

Either I am wrong on this subject or a number of the members of the committee are. In my opinion you do not have to grade any vegetables at all. You can sell any number of any kind of vegetables you wish without grading; but if you do sell vegetables and call them the grades according to this legislation, then they must come up to the standard.
Even if a person is a market gardener, under this legislation his vegetables must be graded and certified.

I do not believe that is the case. If you put these vegetables in a container and mark them as being of a certain grade, then they must come up to that standard and weight, but if there are no grades there are no restrictions.
That depends upon what we have in our regulations.

Any
vegetable that is going to be exported should be graded'. But supposing on ordinary farmer goes to a neighbour for two or three sacks of potatoes to carry him over until his new crop is ready for use, according to this legislation if it passes in its present phraseology, he will have to tag those bags of potatoes and weigh them, the sack will have to be a certain size and on it will have to be the name and address of the man who grew the potatoes. That is all nonsense.
That is not necessary unless he grades them.
The clause refers to "person" instead of "dealer" or "middleman". That is the point to which I wish to draw the attention of the minister.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Barrels to be well filled.

I should like to ask this question of the Minister of Justice who is now in his seat and who in his absence was made responsible for this legislation, because we have had it presented to the committee that this bill has been approved in all respects
by the Department of Justice. What does he think of this pernicious activity on the part of the Minister of Agriculture in providing all these grades, regulations and restrictions with respect to market gardeners, for instance, in Montreal? ?
I was dealing with his deputy minister.

What does the Minister of Justice say in regard to this? ? I think the minister is framing a political issue that will be very attractive to hundreds and even thousands of people in Montreal who are engaged m market gardening, who will now come under these restrictions and whose business will be entirely changed if these provisions are put into force. In fact as that business is now conducted in the markets of Montreal, you are going to fill your courts of sessions with petty criminal cases and your gaols with agricultural criminals.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am a pretty busy man and it is impossible for me personally to study the legislation of all the departments. Apart from that I have such a good feeling for my friend the Minister of Agriculture that I might lack the necessary impartiality and I prefer 'that my deputy and the other officials of any department deal with his proposed legislation. I am told by those officials that the bill as drafted is perfectly legal and constitutional, and I do not think my hon. friend should worry about the political issue that can be raised with regard to it.

Does my hon. friend think the ordinary market gardener who comes into the city of Quebec or Montreal with his team of horses or with his Ford automobile to distribute throughout the city or the outskirts or through the markets the products of his farm, should be compelled, before he can sell his goods, to undergo all this grading and weighing and to put his products on the market in a certain kind of container with an inspection certificate on it, failing which he will be liable to all sorts of fines, forfeitures and penalties? Does my hon. friend think that is wise or expedient legidation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Personally I am not enamoured of too many restrictions. I must admit I believe in freedom of trade. Regarding the inspection ol vegetables for export, I would like to give a hint to the Minister of Agriculture. While inspection is quite necessary, I do not think that this legislation is going to solve all the trouble. We found in western Canada that while we had to market our wheat collectively, and depend on the government to provide the machinery and facilities for the moving of our wheat from the farm to the markets of the world, we did not solve all our troubles until we formed ourselves into what is known as the wheat pool. We have two classes of inspection, the seed potato inspection, and the table stock inspection, each under a different branch of the Department of Agriculture. The inspection for seed potatoes is compulsory. No man can ship certified seed potatoes without having them government inspected and a certificate placed on the sack.
When it comes to shipping table stock, inspection and certificate is not compulsory, but unless the shipment is inspected and certified by the inspector, for which a fee of five dollars is charged, the car cannot go forward as Canada A table stock. This inspection was undertaken voluntarily in Prince Edward Island, and both growers and shippers have found it beneficial. I think I am safe in saying that last year fully 90 per cent of the table stock shipped out of the province was inspected, and that inspection was voluntarily accepted by both the grower and the shipper. The shipper paid the five dollar inspection fee to the inspector, who would then place his certificate on the car. This inspection protects both the grower and the shipper. When those potatoes reach their destination, if the consignee makes any complaint against them, the shipper can produce his certificate of inspection to show that the potatoes were of class A grade when shipped, and it is then up to the consignee to pay for them.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 191, to amend the Criminal Code.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Unlawful association; publishing seditious books, etc.

I would like to ask the Minister of Justice one or two questions in regard to this bill. In the explanatory notes I notice this section is to be repealed, and it seems to be rather lengthy. Apparently when that section was incorporated in our statutes it was considered advisable to put some restraint upon certain organizations, societies or individuals who were propagating certain doctrines or doing certain things in this country. The various matters are specified in the section which is to be struck out, and the severity of the penalties would seem to indicate that when the bill was passed these offences were considered to' be very serious indeed. This bill is very short; it simply states that section 98 is to be repealed, and all these offences and the penalties imposed are to be wiped out. My question is this:	Is there anything in any statute
to take the place of section 98 of the Criminal Code, imposing penalties for any of the offences mentioned under that section, or are we to suppose that the repeal of section 98 gives these persons a free hand in respect to the matters for which formerly they were severely penalized?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A bill similar to this has been adopted by this house five times, and in each case it has been rejected by the other chamber. Section 98, which this bill seeks to repeal, was placed in our statutes in 1919; at that time the sections affected were 97a and 97b, but the number of the section was changed in the revision which took place last year. At the time these two sections were inserted in the Criminal Code it was suggested that there was some unrest in the country; it was just after the war, and it was thought desirable to define certain kinds of what might

Criminal Code Amendment
be called sedition. Sedition is already subject to the disposition of the criminal code and more particularly of the common law. Ever since this amendment of 1919 was adopted the labour community of Canada have felt that it was aimed to prevent them from pursuing their ordinary activities. I do not say that that is the correct interpretation, but I know that since 1921, when I became a member of the government, every year that the Trades and Labour Congress sent delegates to interview the government this was one of the matters which they urged more particularly. They have received advice from the legal advisers of the labour unions to the effect that, by stressing the point the courts might even decide that a strike was an unlawful association under the provisions of that section. I repeat that I do not say they are right in that contention, but this has been a sore spot with them ever since 1919. This house has voted five times to eliminate this section, and we are doing so again this year.
We have already in the code all that is necessary to prosecute for the crimes of sedition, seditious libed, seditious words or unlawful meetings. Section 87 deals with unlawful assemblies; section 130 deals with seditious oaths; section 132 refers to seditious words, seditious li'bel and seditious conspiracy. Under section 135 of the code we have provision with regard to the libel of any foreign sovereign; and in section 136 we have provision against publishing false news. As I said, under the British law sedition is an offence under the common law, and always has been such. In the British parliament it was proposed to define sedition and make it a statutory offence; the commission which was appointed for that purpose reported accordingly, but after a long debate the British parliament came to the conclusion it was better to leave it under the common law as it then was. The same thing has happened in Canada; the commissioners who prepared the Criminal Code had an article defining sedition, but after a long and important debate this house decided to leave it under the common law. That condition continued until 1919, when this amendment was placed in our statutes. At the same time section 133 which existed at that time was repealed and I intend to move an amendment in order to reinsert section 133. This was done last year and in the years previously, and it is only due to a mistake that this bill did not contain that provision. I think the house will see that parliament obviously went too far in 1919 when the section which I am now going to read was repealed:
No one shall he deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in good faith,-
(a)	to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measures; or
(b)	to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of the United Kingdom or of any part of it or of Canada or of any province thereof or in either house of parliament of the United Kingdom or of Canada or in any legislature or in the administration of justice; or to excite His Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure by lawful means the alteration of any matter in the state; or
(c)	to point out, in order to their removal, matters which are producing or have a tendency to produce feelings of hatred and illwill between different classes of His Majesty's subjects.
_ Mr. EDWARDS (Frontenac):	Is that
intended to modify acts already existing?
Mr. LAPOINTE; This was in the code until 1919, but it was repealed at that time, and I desire to reinsert it now. I read the section to show that parliament went too far in repealing it. Surely it is not seditious to criticize acts of a government. We may not like some of the criticism, but I would not go so far as to say that it constituted sedition to blame even the present government for its actions, public or otherwise. We have in the Criminal Code and in the law all that is necessary with respect to the crime of sedition.
Have we ever prosecuted or punished anyone under this section that was repealed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has asked that Question. The officers of my department tell me that to their knowledge no prosecution was ever made.
Since 1919?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Since 1919.

I think it would be a backward step for parliament to pass this bill. Coming from an industrial centre I wish to protest against the repeal of section 98 of the Criminal Code. Communism is rampant in this country to-day. Books are being brought in preaching revolution and European doctrines and economic principles-doctrines which the people here do not want. The Canadian people are opposed to these doctrines both from the standpoint of patriotism and loyalty and from the standpoint of labour itself. I do not believe that the labour organizations of the country approve of the repeal of this section, and this applies particularly to the trades union movement in Canada. The trades union movement has no greater enemy than the red flag of com-
Criminal Code Amendment

munism. In the larger centres of population the communists are preaching revolution; they are advocating the policy, when any strike takes place, of resort to force and other measures of violence. Just look at the sort of freedom that is enjoyed in the United States. Do we want communism in Canada? This country has the utmost freedom and there is no complaint from people who want to assemble lawfully. People can hold meetings in Hyde park whenever they wish to do so, and in the city I come from labour and capital have always got along amicably. The section which this bill seeks to repeal is in my opinion necessary in the interests of labour itself. Our laws are liberal enough as they are and there is no reason why this section should be repealed. Labour and capital in Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, are getting along well to-day. In my opinion this bill is a backward step.

I was not aware that it was the intention of the government to have this bill considered to-night. I am wholly opposed to the passing of it, amending the legislation as it stands at the present time. I think we have to be thankful that we have a senate in Canada, and I trust that the senate, if the bill passes, will again justify its existence by declining to approve it. The reason this law was introduced was, as I remember, that there was no precise categorical definition of sedition, and it was necessary when men undertook to overthrow law and authority by violence to have something definite and to show, when they did advocate the overthrow of government and constituted order by violence, that it was a crime. And it was on the statute books as a crime: they knew what they were doing and if they committed that particular crime they would suffer, and justly so. Let us read just the first clause of section 98:
Any association-
And anyone in this house who objects to this clause should, I think, declare himself, and his constituency should know that he does object to it.
Any association, organization, society or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose purposes is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada-
How?
-by use of force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or by threats of such injury, or which teaches, advocates, advises_ or defends the use of force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, in order to accomplish

such change, or for any other purpose, or which shall by any means prosecute or pursue such purpose or professed purpose, or shall so teach, advocate, advise or defend, shall be an unlawful association.
And such an association shall be subject to the law of -this land. The gist of this matter is the overthrow of authority by force and violence, and I believe there is no one member of this house who is prepared to advocate that in Canada it shall not be an offence to seek by force, violence and terrorism the overthrow of government. Take any other means you like which are perfectly lawful. I resent on behalf of the labour organizations the suggestion that they are a unit in support of this amendment. They are not. There are, of course, some who are anxious, in the interests of communism-rampant communism-to get around this law so that they may not be hampered by it.
Will the hon. member tell me what labour organizations are in favour of retaining this legislation? He has made a definite statement. Will he prove it?

I have made a definite statement and I will prove it. There are labour men in the city I come from, and in Hamilton, who -are just as strongly opposed as I am to the repeal of this law. I do not know the names of the labour organizations, but I am quite sure that a majority of the honest thinking labour m-en of this country are opposed to the repeal of the law as it stands. A short time ago in Port Arthur a case was tried by the Hon. Mr. Justice Kelly, with a result that was staggering to _ him. There was an institution set up which inculcated the destruction by force of government, law and order in Canada. It was taught in the schools on Sunday and they had a wide list of men who were pledged to that very thing. What is the benefit of the law as it stands on the statute books? ? It is simply ' this, that there is a distinct offence defined. Sedition is not defined in the British law so that it is clearly understood by the man on the street. It is a matter for lawyers, a matter wherein lawyers have disagreed and cases have gone from court to court. But here, as I say, is a plain offence, an offence which is clear in the mind of each one of us, and a distinct remedy for it. This house should not only pause but stop and decline to pass such a bill as this. For my part I am surprised-and surprise has been expressed before-tha-t. the Minister of Justice, in the face of offences such as the law as it stands now can deal with readily, seeks to put it into the hands of men to spread bolshevism throughout the country, men who will, if op-

Criminal Code Amendment
portunity is given, attack any government by force, men who seek to humiliate the country and to attack not only governments but any institution which traverses the course they think should obtain, and who instead of doing this in the way we are all proud to have men who hold views_ opposite to ours do, namely, by argument, persuasion or any other lawful means, do it by the dagger, the gun and the bomb. I believe the_ right-minded people of all classes, labour included, are against removing this law from the statute book, and I am unwilling that it should be removed without my protest, as forceful as I can make it. I am sorry it lacks more emphasis, but I will rely upon the sound judgment of the senate if this house, for any reason, is anxious to disturb the law as it exists to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My bon. friend is certainly wrong when he says that the labour people are opposed to the repeal of the section. Year after year, as I have stated, the Trades and Labour Congress have asked for the repeal of this section. Mr. Tom Moore is the distinguished president of that congress and there is no higher-spirited citizen in Canada than Mr. Moore who has given a great deal of assistance in maintaining industrial peace in Canada. This is one of the sections which the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the brotherhoods of railway employees and all the other labour organizations are protesting against; they say that it creates unrest in their ranks and amongst all classes of labour in the Dominion, I may tell my hon. friend that I believe this was hasty legislation, which in a moment of stampede created by a strike in Winnipeg, passed its three readings on the same afternoon and did not receive the attention and consideration it should have received. Therefore it is the duty of parliament to remove it from the statute book, and I do not agree with my hon. friend that the senate is doing its duty in preventing the will of the people, as expressed in the House of Commons from prevailing in Canada.

In the first place I certainly should like to comply with any reasonable request that the labour organizations may make, and no man in this country has a higher opinion of Mr. Tom Moore than I have. The minister is quite right in saying that he has been most helpful in keeping the labour organizations within legitimate lines in endeavouring in a reasonable way, to accomplish their purposes and to bring about what they desire, and I for one should like to see any of his wishes carried out if at all possible. I think I am free to speak with regard to the communists, since I do not belong to the communist party, and since the Independent Labour party to which I belong, has been challenged at the polls by the communists and bitterly denounced. The wildest statements have been made in regard to them not very far from the chamber in which we are now sitting. It has been said that the communists and the One Big Union are one and the same thing. As a matter of fact, if there is any bitter fight being waged at the present time in Canada, it is between the communists and the One Big Union, and any man who confounds two distinct groups in the labour party shows either that he is absolutely ignorant of conditions or that he is wilfully trying to confuse the public mind. We have some dangers in this country, but not the least of these dangers arises from the lack of knowledge on the part of the great majority of the people as to the various labour organizations, and what their objectives really are.
Let me spend a few minutes in reviewing the points that ought to be discussed with regard to this legislation. One of the previous speakers has read the first clause of the section which is being repealed, and he says that no sane man can object to this clause as it stands on the statute book. I want to say that I object to it most decidedly, and in so speaking I am speaking on behalf of the great labour movement of this country, not merely on behalf of some O.B.U. or some Canadian brotherhood organization, or some communist organization, or some left wing organization, or some independent labour party or Canadian labour party, or the Trades and Labour Congress, but on behalf

Criminal Code Amendment
of every one of these organizations, because they all realize that this section is a distinct menace to trade unionists. It says:
Any association, organization, society or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose purposes is to bring about .... any industrial or economic change within Canada, by use of force-
"Any economic change by use of force." Surely a lot of us want economic and industrial changes. Even in this house we want tariff changes, economic changes. The whole point of that paragraph lies in the definition of the phrase, "by use of force." One of the Toronto members said that the Trades and Labour Congress had no worries in this regard. That is not true. I hold in my hand the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada report of their proceedings at the thirty-sixth annual convention, and I find that as far back as that, and every year since, this plea has been reiterated by the congress.
What date is that report?

September 13th to
18, 1920. This report contains a review of this new law which had only a short time before been placed on the statute book, and I find here the legal opinion of Mr. J. G. O'Donoghue, barrister of that city we hear so much about, Toronto, on certain stated questions submitted to him by the executive council of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. This report, I might say, was placed in my hands by Mr. Tom Moore personally several years ago, when we were discussing this matter, and Mr. Moore was urging that we take action along this line. Mr. O'Donoghue says:
The use of these words leaves the door wide open for the prosecution of every trade union in Canada. If "force" is intended to mean "physical force" it should be so stated. The pressure or influence exerted by trade unions is the exercise of "force". That can be interpreted to come within the above section. Read the following extract from Judge Metcalfe's charge to the jury in the Russell case:
That was one of the Winnipeg cases which was in the minds of everyone at the time. Mr. O'Donoghue continues with this extract from Judge Metcalfe's charge to the jury in the Russell case:
"Mr. Russell gave us his idea of a sympathetic strike. He said, 'When a dispute originates between an employer and his employees, and when the labour organizations see that organization being beat, they come to their assistance by calling a strike to force their employers to bring force to bear upon the original disputants to make settlement.' That
is Russell's definition given in the box....
Force, force, force."
Mr. O'Donoghue continues:
Any dictionary will show that "force" has a very wide meaning, covering "influence", "pressure", and the like. If the statute meant "physical force" it would not go on to enumerate "violence" and "physical injury".
A court would be quite justified in interpreting the word in its natural or dictionary sense.
As for the word "terrorism" some light can be thrown upon the interpretation of it, by that given it in the Winnipeg case of Rex v. Russell. There Judge Metcalfe says:
"To walk around about, for instance, to a place where people are employed in large numbers, and to 'boo', gentlemen of the jury, as much terror may be inspired through that as by two or three fighting chaps coming along with bludgeons. Take it from me,^ in strikes you can incite terror without hitting a man over the head. You can incite terror of starvation; you can incite terror of thirst. Is not that quite as effective as inciting by bodily violence? Your stomach will bring you quicker than a crack on the head sometimes. If it is possible that picketing can be done in this country, then the lawful method of picketing is so ineffective that it is a reasonable inference that in a strike of this class, unlawful means would be intended to be applied. Sometimes it has a deterring effect upon people's minds by exposing them to have their motions watched, and to encounter black looks."

May I ask
the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.

Does he
think that any organization in Canada should be permitted to seek economic or industrial changes by violence or injury to persons?

Most decidedly no. But I fancy this section is misunderstood. I say that in time of crisis the word "force" is understood to be violence, whereas it may simply mean such force as is commonly used in a peaceful strike-pressure. That was the interpretation actually given to it in 1919 by the late Judge Metcalfe.

I can quite .appreciate that there might be a very honest misunderstanding in regard to the meaning of the word "force"; but will the hon. gentleman look that over and see if the section could not be changed by cutting out the word "force" so that it would read "violence and injury to persons"?

That would be a
great improvement, but the criminal code already covers it. I do not want to go back over old disputes but, remember this, that an attempt was made to send men out of this country without trial. That is what some of us have been trying to bring before the house again and again. It was in those hectic days that this kind of legislation was put upon the
Criminal Code Amendment

statute books. Now allow me to examine two or three other clauses of this statute. Subsection (2):
Any property, real or personal, belonging or suspected

I want hon. members to note that.
-or suspected to belong to an unlawful association, or held or suspected to be held by any person for or on behalf thereof may, without warrant, be seized or taken possession of by any person thereunto authorized by the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police,
And so on. Let me emphasize that. Any property belonging to or suspected to belong to such an organization may be seized, and that without warrant. In that connection I quote a well-known statement made many years ago by Lord Camden:
Where is the written law,
He asks.
-that gives any magistrate such a power? I can safely answer there is none, and therefore it is too much for us without authority to pronounce a practice legal which would be subversive of all the comforts of society. If suspicion at large should be a ground of search, especially in the ease of libels (i.e. seditious publications), whose home would be safe?
I think hon. gentlemen will surely recognize the reasonableness of our objection to having suspicion as a ground for the seizure of goods.
I proceed to subsection (4):
In any prosecution under this section, if it be proved that the person charged has-
(a)	attended meetings of an unlawful association;
This might mean that if I stopped at a street meeiting 'or went into a hall where a meeting was being conducted by some society that advocated strikes aind similar means of action, and Judge Metcalfe's interpretation was applied, I would be liable to prosecution under this section. This clause (a) is very broad. I have often gone to meetings to find out what was going on or because I had a suspicion that it was of a nature that I did not wanft ito go on, but under those circumstances I might be charged with being a member of the association.
(b)	spoken publicly in advocacy of an unlawful association.
A trade union might be regarded as unlawful.
(c)	distributed literature of an unlawful association by circulation through the post office mails of Canada or otherwise, it shall be presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that he is a member of such unlawful association.
I have always entertained the idea that British justice presumes a man innocent until he is proved guilty. In this case the presump-
tion is that he is guilty until he can prove himself innocent. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is not in harmony with British traditions.
A postman delivering sulch literature would be liable.

Yes. Then subsection (5):
Any owner, lessee, agent or superintendent of any building, room, premises or place, who knowingly permits therein any meeting of an unlawful association-
-becomes liable to a fine or to imprisonment, or to both fine and imprisonment. In practice, labour organizations have found it very difficult to rent buildings because the superintendent or agent was afraid he might get into trouble; and he might very well be afraid. Let me quote subsection (6):
If any judge of any superior or county court, police or stipendiary magistrate, or any justice of the peace, is satisfied by information on oath that there is reasonable ground for suspecting that any contravention of this section has been or is about to be committed, he may issue a search warrant under his hand, authorizing any peace officer, police officer, or constable with such assistance as he may require, to enter at any time any premises or place mentioned in the warrant, and to search such premises or place, and every person found therein, and to seize and carry away any books, periodicals, pamphlets, pictures, papers, circulars, cards, letters, writings, prints, handbills, posters, publications or documents which are found on or in such premises or place, or in the possession of any person therein at the time of such search, and the same, when so seized, may be carried away and may be forfeited to His Majesty.
I do not wish to say anything that would lower the dignity of our various officials, but I think some of us have met stipendiary magistrates and justices of the peace who were not particularly braacLmiindedi, and yet a man of that character may, because of his suspicion, order a man's home to be broken into and his goods seized. I say that is an intolerable situation, and I fancy this -act has remained on the statute book this long simply because no prosecution has ever been attempted under it. Let me go on a little further with subsection (8).
_ Any person who prints, publishes, edits, issues, circulates, sells or offers for sale or distribution any hook, newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture, paper, circular, card, letter, writing, print, publication or document of any kind, in which is taught, advocated, advised or defended, or who shall in any manner teach, advocate, or advise or defend the use, without authority of law, of force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, as a means of accomplishing any governmental, industrial or economic change, or otherwise, shall he guilty of an offence, and liable to imprisonment for not more than twenty years.

Criminal Code Amendment
That is a very broad clause under which it is very easy to convict a man. Further than that, anyone who imports such literature into Canada is liable. Mr. Chairman, I could go into the library of parliament and find fifty books at least on one shelf teaching anarchism, philosophically or otherwise, books which are liable to come under that ban. I know of some books of this character which have been seized in the mail. I know of some people who innocently ordered by mail from Great Britain books which they had seen advertised, and these people can be prosecuted under this section. Yes, my friend from Calgary (Mr. Adshead) suggests; what about the seizure in the public library at Calgary? That, of course, was at this particular period. Books were actually seized from the public library of Calgary which were thought to be seditious; and I know of the case of a man, now a member of the provincial house in Alberta, whose home was violently entered at night and a number of books taken, books which he had brought over from England, many of them books which he had treasured for the past twenty or thirty years. They were seized and he has never been able 'to get them back.
I want to call attention to the safeguards that were in the original Criminal Code. But first a few words as to the definition of sedition. I think I cannot do better than read from a recognized authority, Crankshaw, which every lawyer knows, where the author says:
In section 102 of the English draft code there is, in addition to what is above contained in article 123, a clause defining a seditious intention as,-
"An intention,-
"to bring into hatred or contempt or to excite disaffection against the person of Her Majesty, or the government and constitution of the United Kingdom or of any part of it as by law established, or either house of parliament, or the administration of justice; or to excite Her Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, otherwise than by lawful means, the alteration of any matter in church or state bv law established; or
to raise discontent or disaffection amongst Her Majesty's subjects; or
to promote feelings of ill-will and hostility between different classes of such subjects."
And it goes on to say:
The Canadian code as originally drawn and introduced into parliament contained a clause defining a seditious intention in terms similar to those above quoted from section 102 of the English draft; but the clause ewked a long discussion and a great deal of criticism during the consideration of the bill in committee; and it was ultimately decided to strike out the clause, and leave the definition to common law.
In tracing, with his usual clearness a.nd ability, the history of this most interesting branch of the law, Sir James F. Stephen says,
that there are "two different views of the relation between rulers and their subjects. If the ruler is regarded as the superior of the subjects, as being by the nature of his position presumably wise and good-the rightful ruler and guide of the whole population-it must necessarily follow that it is wrong to censure him openly, that if he is mistaken his mistake should be pointed out with the utmost respect, and that whether mistaken or not no censure should be cast upon him likely or designed to diminish his authority. If, on the other hand, the ruler is regarded as the agent or servant and the subject as the wise and good master who is obliged to delegate his power to the so-called ruler because, being a multitude, he cannot use it himself, it is obvious that this sentiment must be reversed. Every member of the public who censures the ruler for the time being exercises in his own person the right which belongs to the whole of which he forms part. He is finding fault with his servant. If others think differently they can take the other side of the dispute, and the utmost that can happen is that the servant will be dismissed and another put in his place, or perhaps that the arrangement of the household will be modified. To those who hold this view fully, and carry it out to all its consequences there can be no such offence as sedition. There may indeed be breaches of the peace, which may destroy or endanger life, limb or property, and there may be incitements to such offences, but no imaginable censure of the government, short of censure which has an immediate tendency to produce such a breach of the peace ought to be regarded as criminal."
At the present day, when the right of forming political organizations, of holding political meetings, and of giving-through the press, or on the public platform-free expression to our thoughts upon and criticisms of public men and affairs, is so well recognized, a written or printed publication, a public speech, or an assembly, meeting, convention or combination would have to be of an extremely vicious, inflammatory, and dangerous character to form the basis of a successful prosecution for a seditious libel, a seditious speech, or a seditious conspiracy.
Now we removed in 1919 the safeguards which had hitherto existed, and which are intended by the amendment of the Minister of Justice to be replaced upon the statute book. I think no one will suggest that it is not a fair statement that we should have on our statute book a safeguard which provides that:
No one shall be deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in good faith,-
(a)	to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measure; or
(b)	to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of the "United Kingdom, or of any part of it, or of Canada or any province thereof, or in either house of parliament of the United Kingdom or of Canada, or in any legislature, or in the administration of justice; or to excite His Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, by lawful means, the alteration of any matter in the state; or
(e) to point out, in order to their removal, matters which are producing or have a tendency
Criminal Code Amendment

to produce feelings of hatred and ill-will between different classes of His Majesty's subjects.
I am urging that that be replaced. It was cut out in 1919, and we ask that it be again inserted. Labour is asking that, and surely labour is not unreasonable in asking to have restored the safeguards that are in the British code.

Carried.
Progress reported.

May I ask the Minister of Justice if he is going to have this bill reprinted showing the proposed amendments? If not, will he not send a copy at any rate to the leader of the opposition? This is a bill which has been here for weeks and weeks.
